inserts.title: Frame spacing sets the timing resolution
paragraphs: At 500 frames per second, consecutive frames in these recordings are 2 ms apart. The published time labels are measurements of behavior, not spike times recorded from neurons. Catania and Remple's figure 1(b) reports original frame times for one prey capture followed by renewed search. Catania and Kaas's earlier video used 30 frames per second, a coarser resolution of 33 ms per frame.

The measured timing describes a laboratory search sequence, not a fixed rate under every natural condition. Feeding sessions used earthworm fragments as prey, and a contact may start feeding or be followed by another searching movement. Searching and touching alternate throughout each feeding bout.

The timing constrains the time available for extracting information during each encounter. The published timing leaves the neuronal decision unidentified. Whether cortical processing ends when contact ends requires a separate measurement. Events shorter than one 2 ms frame interval fall below the resolution of these time labels.
notes: Frame spacing sets the timing resolution.

At 500 frames per second, consecutive frames in these recordings are 2 ms apart

inserts.title: Corrective contact continues during movement
paragraphs: A mistaken initial movement lengthens handling. Figure 4 of the study shows the star moving away from prey and then making a corrective foveation, and both movements occur inside one feeding episode. The error lengthens handling, and it is interpreted as a movement error rather than a permanent misidentification of the prey.

The correction indicates that useful tactile information can continue to affect movement after the first response starts. The reversal returns the fovea to the same prey item, so the first contact and the correction belong to one feeding episode, which the video records frame by frame.

The video leaves open whether cortex causes the reversal. The motor estimate was calculated in these encounters rather than observed, and the link between cortex and the reversal remains an inference from the timing values. The timing values come from three separate sets of measurements: a typical contact, prior cortical recordings and a motor estimate.
notes: Corrective contact continues during movement.

inserts.title: Incisors and star perform different functions
paragraphs: Incisors are the anterior teeth involved in grasping, and they are not sensory organs. The star detects and positions the target, and the incisors grasp it. These are different mechanical functions, even though both occur within a single brief feeding response that begins with foveal inspection.

Eastern mole incisors served as the reference in the scanning electron microscopy analysis. Figure 3(a–b) of the study sets the reduced star-nosed mole teeth beside them, while Figure 1(c) adds a second high-speed feeding sequence with original time labels from the same study.

The authors propose that selection favored rapid handling. That proposal rests on performance and morphology, while the historical selection process was inferred rather than observed directly in these animals. The reduced incisors sit in a tweezer-like configuration next to the sensing rays.
notes: Incisors and star perform different functions.

A neurite is a neuronal process, and the disk is its terminal part that contacts the Merkel cell, which is a specialized epidermal cell.

Dye brightness in these preparations is treated as evidence of location. It is not converted into a quantitative estimate of membrane current, so the stain shows where a label sits in the tissue and says nothing about how strongly the cell is driven.

These responses were assigned to the complex by their response characteristics, and each recorded axon was not traced to a labeled complex in that study. inserts.title: Map colors encode measured organ density
paragraphs: The heat maps keep the authors' original scale and colors. Their color codes measured organ density, which differs from cortical magnification and from the sensitivity of an individual axon. Organ positions were measured on flattened stars by scanning electron microscopy, and density was computed from those positions.

The published curves are fitted to measured organ positions on flattened stars. The original fitted curves describe anatomy, and they summarize how organ density rises from the star's center outward to the ray tips, passing through the ray bases and middle regions.

The flattened-surface measurements are not recordings of receptor activity during active searching. The density pattern describes where sensory units sit on the surface, and it says nothing about how often each unit fires during a search. Normalized eccentricity places positions from all rays onto one shared axis from base to tip.

inserts.title: Rapidly adapting units go silent in steady contact
paragraphs: A rapidly adapting neuron can remain highly sensitive while becoming silent during an unchanged indentation. Matching responses to terminals relied on the resemblance of response features, with no post-recording identification of every ending. The recordings support multiple peripheral codes for contact, and they leave open whether each code is separately needed for prey discrimination.

inserts.title: Ganglion makeup shapes incoming signals

Differences in that population can change what the brain receives before cortical magnification occurs. The trigeminal ganglion serves the face, while the dorsal root ganglia serve the body, and both were sampled in the same animals.

NF200 labels many large, myelinated sensory fibers, while peripherin labels many small sensory neurons. Figure 1(E) and Figure 1(F) of the study show the trigeminal and dorsal root ganglion labeling alongside their cell fluorescence distributions. Each marker's proportions were reported separately for the two ganglia.

Marker-defined groups are not exhaustive functional categories. Gerhold and colleagues used these markers to choose candidate populations for physiological tests, because facial tissues other than the star also receive input from that ganglion. Cultured neurons from these ganglia were then tested with mechanical and chemical stimuli.

inserts.title: Transcript abundance is several steps from behavior
paragraphs: A transcript must be translated into protein, that protein must act in an appropriate cell, and its activity must contribute to a sensory response. Each of these steps is a place where the expression signal can be lost, so RNA abundance sits several steps from behavior. Bulk ganglion tissue adds supporting cells to the neurons being measured.

Reference transcripts from three other species were used to assemble the expression profiles. Figure 3(A–D) of the study shows the ganglion expression comparison, the functional categories and the channel candidates, and the same candidates were carried forward to qPCR tests.

The expression patterns nominate molecules for functional testing rather than assigning a complete transduction pathway. Reads that failed to match one reference species were passed to the next one in the series. Between 42% and 65% of sequenced reads received an assignment in this way.

paragraphs: Co-labeling places two proteins in the same cellular profiles at the resolution of the assay. Each of the 11 modules marks a territory of neural tissue for one ray. The modules form a star-like pattern inside a relay nucleus, which is a brainstem structure rather than a miniature nose. Module identity follows ray identity, so each module can be read as one ray's territory.

inserts.title: Stripe areas are measured on flattened cortex
paragraphs: A tangential section runs approximately parallel to the cortical surface, so cutting this way exposes a flat sheet of the map. Flattening makes the map easier to measure while changing the tissue's original three-dimensional configuration, and the S1 and S2 stripes both become visible in that sheet.

Figure 10(B–C) of Catania and Kaas (1997) shows the cytochrome-oxidase stripes of S1 and S2 in flattened cortex. Sawyer and Catania's Figure 1(A) shows the 22-ray tactile star whose rays these stripes represent. Electrophysiological mapping tied each stripe to tactile input from the contralateral side of the nose.

Dividing each S1 stripe's area by the number of incoming myelinated fibers gives cortical area per afferent. Ray 11 retained the largest value after this normalization, which distinguishes the foveal territory from the other rays. Cortical area per afferent was measured for each of the rays in the same study.

2: The star-nosed mole, Condylura cristata, searches wetland substrates with 22 fleshy nasal rays. Tactile sensing detects mechanical contact rather than airborne chemicals, so the rays work as touch surfaces that meet the environment directly, rather than as fingers that grasp food. Eleven rays surround each nostril, and matching ray numbers on the two sides describe corresponding positions.

Catania and Kaas filmed captive animals from beneath transparent tunnel floors and scored which rays touched earthworm pieces. Filming from below made each contact visible. Contact first spread across the whole star, and later exploration concentrated on the paired ventral eleventh rays, placed just in front of the mouth. The scored contacts form the basis of the ray-use record.

This directed sampling is a **behavioral specialization** within a single sensory surface. The star supplies broad initial coverage, while a small region repeatedly inspects potential prey, so one organ serves both wide search and close examination. Uniform sampling of the whole star would look different, so the choice of where to sample is part of the specialization.
3: Catania and Remple recorded feeding through a glass-bottom tunnel at 500 frames per second. This **high-speed videography** separated periods of substrate contact from movements between contacts, while the transparent floor kept the star in clear view. Frames at this rate resolve contacts lasting a few tens of milliseconds, so brief touches become countable events.

Search movements lasted about 50 ms and touches about 25 ms, producing approximately 13 contacts per second. A contact could start feeding or lead into another searching movement, so **intermittent sampling** continues even when the animal appears to explore without pause. The alternation of touch and search is the basic rhythm of the feeding sequence.

Earthworm fragments supplied the prey in these recordings, so each encounter is a short sequence of brief contacts. The searching and touching pattern shows how the star gathers information in small, repeated samples. Each sample is short, so the star relies on many successive contacts rather than one prolonged touch. Each brief touch is therefore a sampling event.
4: **Foveation** is movement that places a region of high sensory resolution onto a target. Catania and Kaas scored successive contacts in video recordings of feeding, and the initial contact could involve a lateral ray. The recorded contacts show the star moving to bring a target into the region of highest resolution, which is the defining feature of foveation.

Later contacts brought the prey toward the paired eleventh rays. In individual encounters the entire star changed position until ray 11 touched the item, so the sensory surface itself is actively positioned around the target. The movement is a whole-organ reorientation, not a change in the way one ray moves alone. Each later contact moves the item closer to those rays.

Repeated use of ray 11 justifies calling it a tactile fovea. Its behavior resembles target-directed visual fixation, which makes the tactile fovea a close analogue of the visual system's aiming of the eyes at objects. Both systems place the most sensitive region onto what matters most at that moment. Its function therefore resembles fixation.
5: **Handling time** is the foraging time lost while a predator takes a prey item instead of searching for another. Catania and Remple measured it from the end of the first prey contact until eating finished and the star began another searching movement. This endpoint is set by the resumption of searching, so every trial is timed the same way.

For earthworm pieces 0.8–2.0 mm across, mean handling time was 227 ms, and observed times ranged from 120 to 440 ms. The measured interval included foveation, grasping and consumption, so it spans more than a sensory latency alone. The full sequence of positioning and eating is therefore included in the time. Every trial uses the same endpoints.

These exceptionally short intervals establish rapid performance for small, prepared prey in laboratory conditions. Large prey, environmental obstacles and unsuccessful encounters add other costs, so the 120 ms value describes one well-defined case. Small fragments are the case in which the whole capture sequence stays fast. The sequence ends when the star resumes searching.
6: In a **double take**, the star first moves away from a contacted prey item, then reverses and places the fovea onto it. Catania and Remple identified these sequences in high-speed video and followed the prey position across consecutive frames. The frame-by-frame record keeps the timing of the first movement and of the correction in view.

Double takes occurred in more than one-third of feeding trials. A typical contact lasted about 25 ms, whereas prior cortical recordings placed tactile response onset near 12 ms, and the authors estimated about 5 ms for a motor command to reach the periphery. These three intervals were set side by side in the authors' timing argument.

These timings support the proposal that fast sampling sometimes outruns the completed feeding decision. The motor estimate came from the authors' calculation rather than a direct measurement during these encounters. A **processing-speed limit** is therefore an interpretation of converging evidence from several sources. The timing values come from separate sets of measurements.
7: **Prey profitability** is energy gained per unit handling time. Catania and Remple combined video measurements with published energetic estimates to evaluate small earthworm pieces, and their curves are the authors' published model. Profitability ranks prey by how much energy each item returns for every second spent handling it. The curves are shown as the authors modeled them.

A typical small fragment supplied about 10 J, with handling near 230 ms, giving a reported profitability near 44 J/s. Larger earthworm segments supplied about 1,100 J but took approximately 19 s to handle, which reduced their advantage. The larger segment carries far more energy, yet its long handling time lowers the return per second.

Rapid handling can therefore make tiny prey valuable even when individual items contain little energy. The energetic values were estimates rather than direct calorimetry in each trial, and profitability leaves out search costs. Those costs decide how often a small item is encountered, which is a separate factor from its return. A small fragment can therefore be worth handling.
8: Catania and Remple measured the contact surface from close-up behavioral recordings and set star-nosed moles beside eastern moles, Scalopus aquaticus. Sensory coverage here means the area touched during one sampling event, rather than the sensitivity of an individual receptor. The measurement therefore concerns how much surface a single touch covers. Coverage is distinct from receptor density.

The star contacted about 0.92 cm² per touch, while the eastern mole's snout contacted 0.11 cm². Search rates were about 13 and eight contacts per second, respectively, and combining coverage with rate predicted roughly fourteenfold greater encounter opportunity at equal small-prey density. Both factors together raise the chance of meeting prey in one encounter.

This link between expanded anatomy and search advantage is plausible rather than measured. The encounter estimate assumes equivalent prey distributions and independent sampling, and eastern moles also ate none of the smallest items accepted by star-nosed moles. The eastern mole therefore serves as a reference point for the star's search performance. Eastern moles set the baseline.
9: After foveal inspection, the star-nosed mole captures small prey with its front teeth. Catania and Remple examined the dentition with scanning electron microscopy, which revealed how the teeth are built and arranged. The teeth are the last element in a capture sequence that begins with the star. Dental anatomy was therefore examined in the same study as the sensory surface.

The star-nosed mole's **incisors** are reduced and arranged in a tweezer-like configuration. High-speed sequences associate their use with the final movements of the star during capture of fragments as small as 0.8 mm across, and their proximity to the fovea minimizes the required approach. Because the teeth sit close to the star's sensing region, the grasp follows directly from inspection.

Anatomy and behavior support **coordinated sensory and feeding specializations**. Both features bring the sensing surface and the grasping teeth into one brief sequence, which suits small, quickly handled prey. The two specializations work as parts of one feeding system rather than as separate traits. Both appear in the same high-speed sequences, which ties sensing to grasping.
10: An **Eimer's organ** is a small epidermal sensory unit containing several types of nerve ending. The receptor surface and its nerves therefore develop together. The early nerve pattern precedes the free appendage.
